rungs.title: Person masks and per-view identity
rungs.status: measured (surface): ours 0.52-0.63 IoU, oracle 0.71-0.88, recall falls twice as far as precision

visuals.title: D9b: how well the character covers the person in the photographs
visuals.plain: The reference fitter's person masks are the reference; higher is better, on the frames this step changes. It is LEVEL, and level is the honest answer: the bones move three to six millimetres on a character rasterised at a quarter of the footage's resolution, which is under a pixel on most of the four cameras. This chart is here to catch a regression, not to show the gain -- the gain is in the two charts above. The hatched bars are the build before this step and the reference fitter's own mesh, which is the ceiling a body of the wrong proportions can reach rather than a target.

visuals.title: D8c: how well the body and legs cover the person in the photographs
visuals.plain: The reference fitter's person masks are the reference; higher is better. Torso, legs and head, on the two runs where the hips are wrong. On the collapse run -- three cameras agreeing on hips that are too close together -- the mesh covers measurably more of the person after the repair, and the margin of uncertainty is clear of zero. On the stretch run it does not move at all, and that is expected rather than disappointing: the performer is lying down, only two cameras can see him, and the error is along the one direction those two cameras cannot resolve -- correcting it barely changes any pixel. The hatched bars are the build before this one and the reference fitter's own mesh, which is the ceiling a body of the wrong proportions can reach rather than a target.

visuals.title: D8b: how well the arms cover the person in the photographs
visuals.plain: The reference fitter's person masks are the reference; higher is better. Arms only, and only the 41 frames where the capture goes wrong. The bars are level: this change moves the pixels by less than this instrument can resolve, and every margin of uncertainty spans zero. That is the honest reading -- the photographs neither support nor contradict the step. The hatched bars are the build before this one and the reference fitter's own mesh, which is the ceiling a body of the wrong proportions can reach rather than a target.

visuals.title: D9: how well the arms' outline covers the person's arms
visuals.plain: The reference fitter's person masks are the reference; higher is better. Arms only, everything else taken out. Whole take and the stretch where the two performers overlap. It rises on both performers in both cuts, and on performer 1's overlap stretch the interval is clear of zero. The hatched bars are the build before this one and the reference fitter's own mesh -- the ceiling a body of the wrong proportions can reach, not a target.

visuals.title: D9: the same photographs on performer 1
visuals.plain: Same masks, same two cuts, higher is better. This is the performer whose arms the previous step had the most trouble with, and it is where the rise is largest and the only cell whose interval is clear of zero.

visuals.title: D8: how well the arms cover the person in the photographs, on the frames where it went wrong
visuals.plain: The reference fitter's person masks are the reference; higher is better. Arms only, and only the 41 frames where two of the four cameras have lost a performer -- the frames this step is about. The hatched bars are the build before this one and the reference fitter's own mesh, which is the ceiling a body of the wrong proportions can reach rather than a target. A short window gives a wide margin of uncertainty and that is stated on the technical page.

visuals.title: D7b: how well the body's outline covers the person, by how far they are bent over
visuals.plain: The reference fitter's person masks are the reference; higher is better. Body and legs only, arms taken out, performer 0. It rises in every band and most where they are most bent over, and there the interval is clear of zero. The hatched bars are the build before this one and the reference fitter's own mesh -- the ceiling a body of the wrong proportions can reach, not a target.

visuals.title: D7b: the same photographs on performer 1
visuals.plain: Same masks, same three bands, higher is better. Nothing falls on this performer either; the gain is smaller because this take's pelvis and trunk disagree less.

visuals.title: D7b: the arms in the photographs
visuals.plain: Same masks, higher is better, arms only. The arms move here -- they hang off the chest this step turns -- and the check is that they do not get worse. On both performers the change sits inside the range the measurement itself is uncertain by.

visuals.title: D7: how well the body's outline covers the person, by how far they are bent over
visuals.plain: The reference fitter's person masks are the reference; higher is better. This is the body and legs only, with the arms taken out. On performer 0 it rises in every band and most where they are most bent over, which is what this step was meant to do -- but a deliberately wrong answer, a pelvis frozen bolt upright, rises almost as much on this performer, so the photographs cannot tell the two apart here. The other hatched bar is the reference fitter's own mesh: the ceiling, not a target.

visuals.title: D7: the same check on performer 1, where nothing moved
visuals.plain: Same reference, same three bands, higher is better. On this performer the outline did not change in any band -- and this is the same performer whose hip joint did not move either. The hatched bar is a deliberately wrong answer, a pelvis frozen bolt upright, built and photographed the same way: on this performer, bent over, it loses a fifth of the overlap. So the check has plenty of power here and this step simply costs nothing.

visuals.title: D7: the arms, which this step does not touch and which did not move
visuals.plain: Same masks, higher is better, arms only. This step changes the hips and nothing below the collarbone, and the photographs agree: neither performer's arms moved outside the range the measurement itself is uncertain by.

visuals.title: D3: how well the delivered outline covers the person in the footage, before and after
visuals.plain: MAMMA's person masks are the reference; higher is better. This is the instrument that FELL under D2b. It rose in all eight cells once the mesh carried the same skeleton the joints were solved on. The hatched bar is MAMMA's own mesh through the same rasteriser.

visuals.title: What D2 cost on the photographs: outline overlap before and after
visuals.plain: Each camera's own person mask is the reference, the one measurement here that reads pixels of the footage rather than another model. The skeleton is better placed by every joint measure and the mesh bound to it overlaps worse; the discordance lives in what joins them. MAMMA's mesh through the same renderer is the ceiling.

visuals.title: How much our body outline overlaps the person in the frame
visuals.plain: Each camera's own person mask is the reference. MAMMA's mesh through the same renderer is the best this measurement can reach; a flat rectangle over the person is the wrong answer that must lose.

bars.label: MAMMA's pose on an average body
A flat rectangle over the person

visuals.title: How much of the person our outline covers (recall)
visuals.plain: Ours falls twice as far below MAMMA on recall as on precision: the delivered body is too small and misplaced rather than too big.

rungs.title: 2D landmarks
rungs.status: measured with controls; the coherent bias is ~11 px at 3840, not 18.6, and the verdict is the pseudo-label campaign

visuals.title: Detector error after triangulation, and how much a coordinate fix could remove
visuals.plain: MAMMA's fitted joints are the reference, at zero. The first bar is our detector as it is; the second is after the best honest per-camera shift; the third is the ceiling no shift can beat. Most of the error is per-joint, which is why the next step is training, not offsets.

bars.label: Ours, offsets fitted on other frames

visuals.title: How well the four cameras agree with each other about our detector's points
visuals.plain: No reference at all: the detector against itself across views. Pairing the wrong people across cameras must score far worse, and it does.

visuals.title: Times the two performers were confused for each other
visuals.plain: MAMMA's subject labels are the reference. Zero is the target, and it must still hold when one camera runs a frame early or late.

bars.label: Ours, one camera a frame early
Ours, one camera a frame late

visuals.title: Our triangulation given MAMMA's own 2D points
visuals.plain: MAMMA's exact landmarks are the reference. About 10 mm is the floor the reference itself imposes, so these bars say our geometry reaches it.

rungs.title: Temporal solve and smoothing
rungs.status: measured on synthetic truth (I2, I7): 1.15 mm floor; the solve beats a line 6.7x on burst outages and loses on isolated drops; zero-phase smoother

visuals.title: Our whole pipeline on a perfect detector: how far from the truth it lands
visuals.plain: MAMMA's skeleton projected into the cameras is the exact truth here. The floor is about one millimetre and all of it is the smoothing stage; a rig one frame out of sync costs six times that.

visuals.title: What happens to a joint when only one camera can still see it
visuals.plain: MAMMA's own skeleton projected into the four cameras is the exact truth here, so every millimetre is our reconstruction's. When a joint is lost for a run of frames the sequence solve lands nearly seven times closer than drawing a line through the gap. When the loss is a single isolated frame the line wins instead; the figures below the chart carry that arm.

bars.label: Ours, outages in bursts (real occlusion's shape)
Drawing a line instead, same joints and frames
Frame 0's pose held for the whole take

visuals.title: What the smoothing window does to a bad detection
visuals.plain: Exact truth from our own motion clips, no MAMMA anywhere in this chart. One landmark is thrown off by as much as our own detector's worst 1%; the shipped 300 ms window removes most of the damage, and removing the window leaves it.

rungs.title: Body shape per performer
rungs.status: measured; per-performer rest in the delivery since D3 (2026-09-03)

visuals.title: D3: does the delivered character carry the body the joints were solved on?
visuals.plain: The reference is the track's own forward kinematics, so the right answer is zero. The hatched bar is the exporter as it was before D3, on the same track: it put the mesh's joints about nine centimetres from where every joint instrument scored them.

bars.label: Delivered GLB vs its own FK, performer 0
Delivered GLB vs its own FK, performer 1

visuals.title: D3: a body we built, recovered exactly through the whole delivery
visuals.plain: Synthetic truth is the reference. Six bodies with every bone length, span and spine segment drawn independently, posed, solved, exported and read back. The hatched bar is the same body arriving canonical downstream, which is what shipped before D3.

visuals.title: D3: the rig's shoulder span, fixed rig against the performer's own
visuals.plain: Limb lengths measured from our own capture are the reference. The fixed rig was 540 mm across the shoulders; the delivered body is now each performer's own width.

visuals.title: How far each body's limb lengths are from the performer's own
visuals.plain: Limb lengths measured from our own capture are the reference. A body fitted to the performer should sit well below our one-size rig.

visuals.title: D9b: does each bone point where it was told to point?
visuals.plain: After every bone had been aimed, the automatic floor-contact step slid the whole character sideways to plant a foot -- and the bones kept pointing along the lines they were aimed along from where they used to be. This chart measures, on the frames that slide happens, how far each bone's target sits off the line the bone actually points along. Lower is better and zero is achievable exactly. The hatched bars are the build before this step.

visuals.title: D9b: the same question on the other performer
visuals.plain: The second performer's feet are planted on far fewer frames -- 22 of 150 against 67 -- so the change touches less of his take, and on the frames it does touch the picture is the same. Lower is better.

visuals.title: D9b: the worst single frame in the whole take
visuals.plain: Medians hide the bad frames, so this is the worst frame of 150 rather than the middle one, and it counts only the part an aim can actually fix -- a bone can be too short for its target, and no amount of aiming cures that. Lower is better. After the change the worst frame of the take is three ten-thousandths of a millimetre, which is the storage precision of the delivered file itself.

visuals.title: D9b: measured against a known answer, and against a gauge that cannot see the fix
visuals.plain: Six synthetic bodies of known proportions, posed through our own maths and put back through the real pipeline, so the right answer is known exactly. Lower is better. The solid bars are the arms measured where they really are in the world. The first hatched bar is the SAME delivered bodies scored through the older gauge, which lines each frame up on the hips before measuring -- that removes exactly the sideways slide this step is about, so it reports the corrected arms as worse. Both readings are honest and they answer different questions; the older band is left where it is. The last hatched bar is the legs, which this step does not touch: their error is the cost of planting a foot the truth is still moving, and it is handed to the step that owns it.

visuals.title: D8c: how far the delivered character actually moved
visuals.plain: Read from the delivered files themselves, with the automatic floor-hoist taken out so a re-levelling is not counted as the body moving. This is NOT an error -- there is no correct answer to compare against on this footage. It is the size of the change: on the frames the rule acts on, the character's root moves about three millimetres on the falling performer and not at all on the other, whose hips were never withheld.

visuals.title: D9: how far the delivered elbow and wrist sit from the ones we measured, performer 0
visuals.plain: Our own measured elbow and wrist are the reference, at zero; lower is better. Blue is what this step delivers. The hatched bars are the build before it, which aimed each arm bone by the line between two measured points while the bone actually turns about a joint somewhere else -- so the whole arm was carried off by that gap. The aqua bars are the floor: the part of the miss that a bone of fixed length can never remove, whatever it is aimed at. Blue sits on the floor, so there is nothing left here for an aim to fix; the rest is an arm cut to this performer, and that is a later step.

bars.label: Elbow, ships (aim from the arm's own joint)

visuals.title: D9: the same check on performer 1
visuals.plain: Same reference, same unit, lower is better. This performer's arms start further out and come back the same way. The floor is higher here, and the delivered arm sits on it: on the left elbow the floor is 8.8 mm and the delivery reads 9.1, which is as close as a fixed-length bone can get.

visuals.title: D9: the right arm, both performers
visuals.plain: Same reference, lower is better. Both arms are changed the same way and both land on their own floor, which is the point: this is one rule applied twice, not a fit to one arm.

visuals.title: D9: the shoulder, the neck and the knee, which this step must not touch
visuals.plain: Same reference, same unit, lower is better. This step aims two bones in each arm and nothing else, so every pair of bars here has to be identical -- and they are, float for float, read from the delivered files. The shoulder is still 10-13 mm from the measured shoulder, and that miss is not this step's: it comes from the collarbone having one fixed length, and it is a later step's to close.

visuals.title: D7b: how far the delivered neck sits from the neck we measured, performer 0
visuals.plain: Our own measured neck is the reference, at zero; lower is better. Blue is what this step delivers. The hatched bar is the build before it, which moved the neck off its landmark. The aqua bars are the build before THAT and the floor -- the part of the miss that a straight, rigid spine can never remove whatever it is aimed at. Blue sits on the floor, so there is nothing left here for an aim to fix; the rest is a bendable spine, and that is a later step.

bars.label: Ships (aim from the spine's own origin)
Before D7b: the pelvis frame alone
Floor: what a rigid straight spine cannot beat

visuals.title: D7b: the same check on the third of frames where performer 0 is most bent over
visuals.plain: Same reference, same unit, lower is better -- but only the frames where the performer is most bent over, which is where a pelvis that disagrees with the trunk does the most damage. The neck comes back from 131 mm to 42, and 42 is the floor.

bars.label: Ships (aim from the spine's own origin)
Before D7b: the pelvis frame alone
Floor: what a rigid straight spine cannot beat

visuals.title: D7b: the same check on performer 1
visuals.plain: Same reference, lower is better. This performer is bent over for most of the take, and the neck returns from 44 mm to 18 -- again exactly the floor.

bars.label: Ships (aim from the spine's own origin)
Before D7b: the pelvis frame alone
Floor: what a rigid straight spine cannot beat

visuals.title: D7b: the hips, knees and ankles, which this step must not touch
visuals.plain: Same reference, same unit, lower is better. This step changes the chain ABOVE the hips and nothing below them, so every pair of bars here has to be identical -- and they are, float for float, read from the delivered files. That is the check that stops a good neck being bought with a worse lower body.

visuals.title: D7b: the wrist, on the frames where performer 0 is most bent over
visuals.plain: Same reference, lower is better. Nothing was aimed at the arms here -- but the arm hangs off the chest, so moving the chest back onto the body carries the whole arm with it and the elbow and wrist are then re-solved onto their own landmarks. This is that, and it was predicted before the numbers.

visuals.title: D7: how far the delivered pelvis is from the true pelvis, on bent frames
visuals.plain: Exact synthetic truth is the reference, at zero; lower is better. Blue is what ships. Orange is what the code did before -- the pelvis welded to the trunk. The hatched bar is a deliberately wrong answer: a pelvis frozen upright. It was supposed to lose and it did not, which is why this step's own gate says FAIL.

visuals.title: D7: is the lower-spine landmark stable enough to build a pelvis on?
visuals.plain: No reference at all here -- a bone does not change length, so the spread of a segment's length over the take is how much the detector wobbles. Lower is better. The hatched bars are the body parts this project already trusts; the candidate has to be no worse than the worst of them.

visuals.title: D7: how far the rig's hip joint sits from the hips we measured, on bent frames
visuals.plain: Our own captured hip midpoint is the reference, at zero; lower is better. Before D7 the offset leaned with the trunk. This is REPORTED and not a pass/fail: a frozen answer could drive it to zero without being right.

visuals.title: D3: where the delivered rig lands on our own capture, before and after
visuals.plain: Our own capture is the reference, root-relative. Before: the fixed rig. After: the rig sized to the performer, which is now what ships.

visuals.title: Distance from MAMMA's joints, 15 body joints
visuals.plain: MAMMA's joints are the reference, at zero. Our raw capture, and the same capture driving a parametric body, on identical frames.

visuals.title: What the retarget costs on the arms, and how much sizing the rig recovers
visuals.plain: Our own capture is the reference. The last bar per performer is the converter's own floor, a round trip on a body built to the rig's proportions; nothing above it is proportions.

visuals.title: D2: where the arm root lands on the delivered character, before and after
visuals.plain: Our own capture is the reference, root-relative. Before: the collarbone aimed from a made-up point on the spine. After: aimed from the joint it pivots about, with the rig's hips placed on the captured hips. The legs are shown to prove they did not move.

visuals.title: D2: the converter's own round trip on a canonical body, arms
visuals.plain: A body built to the rig's proportions is the reference, so the right answer is zero. Before: the known clavicle cost. The hatched bar is the best any constant on the spine could do, which never reaches the band. After: the rig's own geometry, no constant.

visuals.title: D2: the same converter on MAMMA's own joints, arms
visuals.plain: MAMMA's rigid skeleton fed through the converter and scored against itself: a separate reference from our capture, never on one axis with it. MAMMA reports here and selects nothing.

visuals.title: What D2 cost and D2c gave back: frames where a collarbone or arm joint turns faster than a human joint can
visuals.plain: A physical ceiling of 800 degrees per second is the reference. Aiming the collarbone from a pivot only 100 to 160 mm from its landmark turns landmark wander into angle; the hatched bar is the collarbone fix alone. D2c rejects frames a collarbone cannot reach at that speed and re-solves the arm below. MAMMA's collarbones through the same measure never approach the ceiling. The median step is unchanged, which is the lever and not this step's to fix.

visuals.title: D2c on synthetic truth: collarbone error on a body whose true motion is known, worst frames
visuals.plain: Exact synthetic truth is the reference: our own motion through the real cameras with the detector's measured noise injected, so the right answer is known. The 95th percentile of the collarbone's error is shown; the median is unchanged because the reject touches 2 percent of frames. The hatched bar is a heavy smoother, which scores better here and destroys 64 percent of true peak speed, which is why it is the wrong answer.

rungs.title: Hands
rungs.status: measured: 36.5 mm held-out, degenerate hands rejected; the shipped hand is under-smoothed

visuals.title: The hand fit scored on a camera it never saw, per hand
visuals.plain: No truth on disk: each hand is fitted on three cameras and scored on the fourth, then rotated. MAMMA's own hand through the same protocol sits above ours because of a skeleton convention gap, so this chart proves the gate rejects a frozen hand; it does not rank us against MAMMA.

visuals.title: Fingertip jitter: how much the fingers shake frame to frame
visuals.plain: The thrash figure. Beside each hand is the part of the shake that is the whole wrist moving rather than the fingers, which is a floor under it. MAMMA's fingertips shake about 0.2 mm on this scale and sit on a different skeleton, so they are not drawn.

rungs.title: Head orientation
rungs.status: measured; thorax window now 9 (synthetic truth, 2026-09-02): medians improved on both performers, p95 mixed, the gate's own floor rose, performer 0 flipped PASS -> FAIL on p95

visuals.title: How closely the head follows MAMMA's, relative to the chest
visuals.plain: MAMMA's head in our chest frame is the reference. MAMMA's own head through our frames is the floor; a head that never moves is the wrong answer that must lose.

visuals.title: How far above the floor the head sits, once the frame's own jitter is cancelled
visuals.plain: Our head's worst-case (p95) disagreement minus MAMMA's own head scored through the same frame, on identical bootstrap draws. This is the figure a change to the chest frame cannot move, and the one ground truth would turn into a target.

rungs.title: Feet, toes and ground contact
rungs.status: measured against MAMMA; a constant 17-24 deg inward toe offset on every foot

visuals.title: How closely each foot follows MAMMA's, once the constant offset is removed
visuals.plain: MAMMA's foot direction in the shin frame is the reference. Its own foot through our frames is the floor; a foot welded to the shin is the wrong answer that must lose. The constant offset is reported separately: our toes point about twenty degrees inward.

rungs.title: Mesh and delivered skeleton -- the end-to-end rung, deliberately last
rungs.status: measured; faces the right way since 2026-09-02 (D1: the naming mirror relabelled at five sites)

visuals.title: D3: the delivered character against MAMMA's joints, before and after
visuals.plain: MAMMA's joints are the reference, at zero; agreement with an instrument, not accuracy. Before: the fixed rig. After: the performer's own body. The aqua bar replays the new rotations on the old fixed rig, which is what a consumer that ignored the skeleton would show.

visuals.title: D2: the delivered character against MAMMA's joints, arms and legs kept apart
visuals.plain: MAMMA's joints are the reference, in absolute world coordinates, so unlike the root-relative charts this one can see where the character actually stands. Agreement with another instrument, not accuracy. The arms improve a lot and the legs a little, as written down before the numbers.

visuals.title: The delivered character against MAMMA's joints, end to end
visuals.plain: MAMMA's joints are the reference, at zero, the same reference as the pose rung. The gap between the fixed rig and the sized rig is the body; the rest is everything above compounded.

visuals.title: Which way the delivered character faces, part by part
visuals.plain: +1 means a part points the same way the performer does in the footage; -1 means exactly the opposite way. Since the 2026-09-02 fix every part points with the performer; before it the pelvis, chest, head and the mesh's own nose read -0.9 to -1.0 while the feet were right. The hatched bar, our capture turned 180 degrees, is what backwards looks like on this scale. MAMMA's independent reading of the performers is the ceiling a head can reach.
